title-group.article-title: Experimental Design and Performance Evaluation of a Solar-Assisted Wearable Cooling Vest With Dual Forced-Air Ventilation

abstract.p: Lightweight personal thermal-management systems are attractive for outdoor heat exposure where space cooling is unavailable. A low-power, solar-assisted garment with dual forced-air ventilation was fabricated and tested outdoors on a single day (08:00–16:00; $n$ = 9 nominal hourly observations, eight elapsed one-hour intervals) at ambient temperatures of 32.5–43.1 ℃, relative humidity of 20–34%, and solar irradiance of 420–950 W/m$^2$. The apparent fan-OFF/fan-ON garment-temperature contrast, $\Delta T_{\text{g}}=T_{\text{OFF}}-T_{\text{ON}}$, was positive at all nine observations, with a mean of 3.89 ± 0.97 ℃ and a maximum of 5.0 ℃ at 14:00. Based on the reported combined airflow and $\Delta T_{\text{g}}$, the estimated sensible cooling rate was $\dot{Q}_{\text{s,est}}$ = 38.43–99.52 W (nine-point mean 75.08 W), and the ventilation cooling performance ratio was VCPR = $\dot{Q}_{\text{s, est}}/P_{\text{fan}}$ = 13.72–35.54 (nine-point mean 26.81); these are engineering screening estimates rather than calorimetric measurements or refrigeration coefficient of performance (COP) values. Trapezoidal integration over the eight elapsed one-hour intervals gave a fan-energy demand of 22.40 Wh, a photovoltaic (PV) panels contribution of 13.08 Wh, and an auxiliary-energy requirement of 9.33 Wh. The PV contribution therefore accounted for 58.4% of the fan-energy demand during the test period. Single-day associations with the ambient conditions are reported descriptively, without causal interpretation. The results provide proof-of-concept evidence of a consistent apparent garment-temperature contrast and a quantified partial PV load offset under the hot-dry conditions tested, and they define an 11.19 Wh storage target for autonomous daytime operation.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Physical performance, concentration, comfort and occupational safety are compromised by exposure to heat, especially when the task is undertaken outdoors for extended periods in hot, dry climates [1], [2], [3]. Personal thermal management systems focus on the microenvironment near the body and can help to decrease reliance on space conditioning. The following methods have been developed: phase change garments, liquid based garments, thermoelectric devices and fan assisted ventilation [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11].

Liquid and thermoelectric systems can provide active cooling, but they require pumps, tubing, heat exchangers, heat sinks, or a relatively large electrical supply [12], [13], [14], [15]. Fan-assisted garments, on the other hand, are mechanically simpler, because low-power fans circulate air within the garment microclimate to aid convective and evaporative heat transfer when ambient conditions are suitable [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21]. Direct evidence that a small, body-mounted photovoltaic (PV) module can supply part of the electrical load of a wearable system is available from two lines of work: wearable-scale flexible PV panels mounted on the body delivered an average of approximately 65 mW and a peak of approximately 94 mW under outdoor irradiance and were proposed explicitly as a battery-supplementing supply for body-worn electronics [22], and solar-powered thermoregulatory clothing has been demonstrated in which an integrated PV layer drives the thermal-management element of the garment using sunlight alone [23]. Because the electrical power delivered by such a module depends on its electrical operating point and on its own temperature, an explicit treatment of the PV thermal behaviour is required when the module is mounted on a garment exposed to high irradiance [24], [25]; PV sizing studies for small stand-alone direct-current loads provide the corresponding framework for matching the daily PV yield, the load demand, and the required storage capacity [26].

This work analyzes a physically fabricated proof-of-concept garment that combines two separate axial fans with direct PV assistance. This study is limited to direct observations of the garment microclimate and the electrical power balance. It does not claim physiological cooling, improved thermal comfort, or a refrigeration-cycle coefficient of performance (COP).

sec.title: 2.1. Existing wearable-cooling approaches
sec.p: Wearable cooling technologies differ in cooling capacity, duration, mass, complexity, and electricity consumption. Phase-change systems have finite latent-heat storage; liquid-circulation systems provide cooling but require pumps and tubing; thermoelectric systems provide local active heat pumping but require hot-side heat rejection; passive garment systems are highly sensitive to radiative and environmental boundary conditions; and forced-air systems have low electrical demand but are sensitive to airflow distribution and ambient humidity. Table 1 positions the present prototype relative to these approaches.

sec.title: 2.2. Research gap and objective
sec.p: The feasibility of wearable cooling garments based on vented, phase-change, liquid, thermoelectric, and multimodal technologies has been established in controlled laboratory and workplace studies [8], [9], [13], [27], [28]. However, fewer studies explicitly report a matched thermal record and an explicit daytime electrical balance for a low-complexity, garment-mounted PV/dual-fan configuration at air temperatures above 40 ℃. The objective of this study is therefore to quantify (i) the apparent fan-OFF/fan-ON garment-temperature contrast, (ii) the estimated sensible cooling rate and the associated ventilation cooling performance ratio (VCPR) screening index, and (iii) the fraction of the fan-energy demand supplied by the PV module over the recorded eight-hour period. A further aim is to provide a transparent chain from the archived observations to a storage-sizing target, in which observed, exactly derived, and assumption-based quantities are kept separate (Section 3).

sec.title: 3.1. Prototype configuration
sec.p:
The prototype consisted of a lightweight outer garment with a hood, two small axial fans placed at two different locations on the lower torso, a PV panel attached to the outer garment, electrical wiring, and leads for the temperature sensors (Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4). The combined reported demand of the two fans was 2.80 W at a nominal voltage of 5 V. Part of this load was supplied by the PV panel, and the remainder was supplied by an auxiliary source. The archived dataset reports a combined airflow of 57–62 m
3
/h for the dual-fan system. Because the airflow instrument and measurement plane were not preserved in the experimental archive, this series is used only as an input to the screening calculation defined in Section 3.4.

sec.title: 3.3. Outdoor test protocol and comparison basis
sec.p: The archived photographs show the garment without a wearer or a thermal manikin (Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4). The reported temperatures therefore describe an unworn garment microclimate and should not be interpreted as skin temperature, physiological strain, or perceived comfort. The single daytime run provided nine nominal one-hour time points and eight elapsed one-hour intervals.

Each tabulated record contains a fan-ON value and a fan-OFF value at each nominal time. The retained record does not establish whether the fan-ON and fan-OFF values were obtained simultaneously, successively, or in an alternating sequence, nor whether the same garment specimen was used for both operating states. No separate stabilization interval was recorded. Hence, the operating-state contrasts are reported only as within-pair contrasts tabulated for the same nominal time; they are not described as randomized, independent, steady-state, or unbiased treatment effects.

No replicate-run dataset is available; the archive contains a single test day. No compass azimuth or quantitative panel-tilt record is available. The photographs show the PV module suspended vertically and facing the sun at the time the photographs were taken. Accordingly, no orientation-specific claim is made, and outdoor variability, possible state-order effects, and the lack of independent replication are treated as design constraints.

The two operating states and the nine consecutive readings are not assumed to be statistically independent, because the outdoor temperature, humidity, irradiance, and time varied together. Comparisons are therefore limited to the recorded operating range and are described as single-day exploratory observations.

sec.title: 4.4. Eight-hour energy balance and photovoltaic output
sec.p:
PV output increased from 0.85 W at 08:00 to a maximum of 2.10 W at 13:00, which coincided with the peak irradiance of 950 W/m
2
(Table 6 and Figure 11). The maximum PV output corresponded to 75% of the instantaneous fan demand of 2.80 W, with the remaining 0.70 W supplied by the auxiliary source. The hourly values in Table 6 are instantaneous powers (W), whereas the integrated quantities are energies (Wh). The energy balance was obtained by trapezoidal integration over the eight one-hour intervals between the nine observations (Eq. (5)); it gives a fan-energy demand of 22.40 Wh, a PV contribution of 13.08 Wh, and an auxiliary-energy requirement of 9.33 Wh. The PV contribution therefore accounted for 58.4% of the fan-energy demand (Figure 11).

sec.title: 4.5. Combined interpretation
sec.p:
The largest apparent garment-temperature contrast (4.8–5.0 ℃ at 13:00–14:00) coincided with high ambient temperature and high irradiance, when the PV module supplied 2.0–2.1 W. The maxima of
Q ˙
s,est
and VCPR also occurred at 14:00; this coincidence is arithmetic, because both indices are calculated from
Δ
T g
and the reported airflow, and it is not presented as independent confirmation. The single-day record does not allow the influences of ambient temperature, humidity, irradiance, time of day, garment state, and any unrecorded change in orientation or wind to be separated. The findings therefore represent an internally consistent operating-state contrast and electrical balance, not an environmental cause-and-effect relationship.

For context, the reported combined airflow of 57–62 m
3
/h (15.8–17.2 L/s) is of the same order as the 12 L/s fan ventilation [29], in which fan ventilation increased total torso cooling by 137–251%. Because the present garment was unworn and the airflow measurement plane was not documented, these values are not directly comparable; the comparison indicates only that the airflow level of the prototype lies within the range examined in controlled ventilation-garment studies.

sec.title: 5. Practical implications and design improvements
sec.p: This eight-hour balance can be directly converted into the storage requirement. So the daytime auxiliary-energy deficit is 9.325 Wh and the engineering reserve is 20%, meaning that the minimum usable storage is 11.19 Wh. Prior to converter, wire, ageing and temperature derating, a capacity of 2.24 Ah at 5 V or 0.93 Ah at 12 V. These nominal values, therefore, need to be surpassed by the selected battery capacity by considering the actual conversion efficiency and the allowable depth of discharge. This sizing result is more descriptive than a statement of full solar autonomy: the PV source was able to provide 58.4% of the fan energy demand for an 8-hour period, but was unable to provide the entire 2.80 W demand for any time period. A design well suited for the field should thus incorporate a charge controller, an energy buffer, protected wiring, washable detachable electronics, acoustic and garment-mass measurements, and repeatable through-garment airflow mapping. To advance from proof of concept, future experiments should feature matched exposure, fixed orientation, a prespecified stabilization criterion, repeated exposures on separate days, ambient and garment temperature sensors being shielded and co-located, and measured inlet–outlet air temperatures. Any reference to skin temperature, comfort, physiological strain or occupational protection should always be followed by a thermal-manikin or ethics approved wearer protocol.

sec.title: 6. Limitations
sec.p: This study consists of nine replications (observations) that are serially ordered. No records of fan-OFF/fan-ON sequencing, stabilization period, garment azimuth, PV tilt or repeat runs are available. The parameters listed above are not included in the archived files, which include the instrument manufacturer, model, range, resolution, stated accuracy, calibration/reference checks, exact sensor coordinates, the plane of airflow sampling, and the path of electrical power acquisition.

These items are therefore reported as unavailable metadata rather than replaced by assumed specifications, and no metrological uncertainty or calibrated-performance claim is made. The garment was not evaluated with a wearer, and no conclusions are drawn regarding skin temperature, thermal sensation, comfort, physiological strain, or occupational safety. The apparent fan-OFF/fan-ON garment-temperature contrast is not an inlet-to-outlet air-temperature difference. Therefore,
Q ˙
s,est
and VCPR are screening indices based on assumed air properties and the reported airflow; they are not direct calorimetric measurements and should not be regarded as refrigeration COP values. No performance value is reported as COP or COP
eff
. The radiation shielding and exposure of the ambient and garment sensors were also not documented:
T ON
was 0.5–3.3 ℃ below the recorded
T amb
, whereas
T OFF
was 1.6–2.4 ℃ above it. Because such cross-series differences may reflect different sensor exposure, only the within-garment contrast
Δ
T g
is interpreted, and garment-to-ambient differences are not used in any derived quantity. Finally, the single-day correlations are confounded by time and by co-varying weather variables; they cannot establish causal effects or support prediction beyond the observed ranges.

sec.title: 7. Conclusions
sec.p:
A dual-fan, PV-assisted garment prototype was tested outdoors during a single hot-dry day from 08:00 to 16:00. The apparent fan-OFF/fan-ON garment-temperature contrast,
Δ
T g
, was positive at all nine observations, with a mean of 3.89 ± 0.97 ℃ and a maximum of 5.0 ℃ at 14:00. Under the stated screening assumptions, the estimated sensible cooling rate,
Q ˙
s,est
, ranged from 38.43 to 99.52 W, while VCPR ranged from 13.72 to 35.54 (nine-point means of 75.08 W and 26.81, respectively). These values are engineering screening indices rather than direct calorimetric measurements or refrigeration COP values; replacing the fixed air density with a temperature-dependent value changed the mean
Q ˙
s,est
by only -1.9%. The eight-hour trapezoidal electrical balance gave a fan-energy demand of 22.40 Wh, a PV contribution of 13.08 Wh, and an auxiliary-energy requirement of 9.33 Wh, corresponding to a PV contribution of 58.4%. The corresponding usable energy-buffer target is 11.19 Wh, including a 20% reserve. Results appear to show a garment-temperature contrast and the partial PV load offset, but not a measured rate of heat removal or an environmental cause-and-effect relationship. Before the results can be generalized, traceable, replicated, and counterbalanced tests are required.
